newsitem.title: GERMANY: German retailers push for tax cuts to spark growth.
newsitem.headline: German retailers push for tax cuts to spark growth.

text.p: Germany's retail sector, saying that longer shop hours have not created new jobs, on Wednesday pressed government officials for tax cuts and labour reforms to break a four-year sales slump.

In a roundtable with Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, retail organisations said eliminating a corporate trading tax and lowering employer contributions to social security programs could lead to millions of new jobs over the next decade.

German service companies should add one million new jobs in that time, but the figure could rise to four million if German companies had conditions like those in the U.S., Michael Fuchs, president of the BGA wholesalers federation, said.

"The employment motor of services is not running on all cylinders in Germany," Fuchs said. "The best way would be to have a dynamic like in the U.S. That would mean the creation of four million additional jobs."

The HDE retail federation said a series of tax increases since German unification had weakened consumer purchasing power. It said income tax cuts would give retail the revenue growth it needs to hire more workers.
Stores have not hired extra workers since shop hours were extended to 8 p.m. on weekdays and 4 p.m. on Saturdays, said the BAG, which represents department stores.
New jobs could appear later this year after after retailers have had time to assess how much business they can expect with later hours on long, summer evenings.
The retail union DAG maintained structural changes in retail companies would improve the jobs outlook. Jobs must come from a redistrubution of the work that is done now, DAG said.
